title: Kid‑Safe Herb Cutting: Supervised Projects with Multi‑Blade Scissors
keyword: kid safe herb cutting with scissors
meta_description: Teach your children kitchen skills safely! Learn how to manage kid safe herb cutting with scissors and the best way to use multi-blade herb shears.
html:
Getting kids involved in the kitchen is one of the best ways to encourage them to eat more greens. However, the knife block is usually off-limits for the little ones. That is where the magic of kid safe herb cutting with scissors comes in. By swapping a chef's knife for a specialized tool, you can give your children a sense of autonomy in meal prep without the high-stress worry of a slip of the blade.

I've found that children are naturally drawn to tools that feel like a "gadget." When you introduce a multi-blade tool, it turns a chore into a game. The goal isn't just to get the cilantro chopped; it's to build their confidence and fine motor skills in a controlled environment.

Choosing the Right Tools for Kid Safe Herb Cutting with Scissors

Not all scissors are created equal. Standard kitchen shears are great for cutting chicken breasts or parchment paper, but they aren't ideal for teaching children how to mince herbs. For a supervised project, I highly recommend using the Herb Scissors. These are five-blade herb shears that mince cilantro, chives, and basil in one snip, which means the child doesn't have to perform a hundred tiny cuts to get a handful of herbs.

The multi-blade design is a game-changer for kids because it reduces the repetitive motion and the time the blades are in active use. Plus, these specific Herb Scissors come with a cleaning comb, which allows you to show your kids the importance of cleaning up after a project—a crucial part of any kitchen lesson.

Preparing the Workspace for Supervised Cutting

Before you hand over the shears, set the stage for success. A cluttered counter leads to accidents. Clear a dedicated space and place a large plastic cutting board or a shallow bowl in front of your child. This contains the "herb confetti" and gives them a clear boundary for where the cutting happens.

Gather your herbs in small bundles. If you are using basil or cilantro, tie them loosely with a piece of kitchen twine or hold them in a tight bunch with your fingers (keeping your hand well away from the blades). This prevents the herbs from scattering and allows the child to focus on the rhythmic motion of the snip.

Step-by-Step: The Multi-Blade Mincing Method

When teaching your children how to use the Herb Scissors, start with a demonstration. Show them how to hold the handle firmly and how to open and close the blades in a smooth, controlled motion. Avoid "rapid-fire" snipping; instead, encourage a steady pace.

Here is the best workflow for a supervised herb project:

  • Wash and Dry: Have the kids help wash the herbs. Ensure they are patted dry with a paper towel, as wet herbs can clump together and stick to the blades.
  • The Grip: Teach them to hold the herb bundle vertically.
  • The Snip: Guide them to snip from the top of the bundle downward.
  • The Collection: Let them use their hands to gather the minced herbs into a pile, which helps them feel the texture of the food.
  • The Cleanup: Use the included cleaning comb to remove the trapped bits of greenery from the five blades.

Best Herbs for Beginner Snips

Some herbs are easier to work with than others. For those just starting with kid safe herb cutting with scissors, I suggest starting with chives. They are thin, sturdy, and don't bruise easily, making them perfect for the five-blade action of the Herb Scissors.

Once they master chives, move on to parsley or cilantro. These have a bit more volume and provide a satisfying "crunch" when cut. Basil is wonderful for flavor, but remind your kids that basil leaves are delicate. If they squeeze too hard, the leaves can bruise and turn black, so this is a great time to teach them about a "gentle touch" in the kitchen.

Safety Rules for the Junior Chef

Even with a safer tool, guidelines are non-negotiable. Establish a "safety zone"—an arm's length of space around the child where no one else is allowed to stand. This prevents accidental bumps that could lead to a mishap.

Always insist that the scissors be passed handle-first. This is a fundamental kitchen safety rule that will serve them well when they eventually move up to using larger knives. Finally, make the cleaning process a mandatory part of the activity. Using the cleaning comb not only maintains the tool but reinforces the idea that the job isn't done until the equipment is clean.

FAQ

Are multi-blade scissors safer than a knife for children?

While no cutting tool is completely without risk, multi-blade shears are generally safer for supervised use because they require less precision and a different grip than a knife. They eliminate the need for the "claw grip" and the risk of a blade slipping across a cutting board toward a finger.

How do I stop herbs from sticking to the blades?

The key is to ensure the herbs are completely dry before cutting. If they are still sticking, a quick rinse with warm soapy water and a pass with the cleaning comb provided with the Herb Scissors will clear the blockage.

What age is appropriate for this activity?

Most children aged 5 and up can handle supervised herb cutting, provided they have the motor skills to open and close the handles. Always maintain a 1:1 adult-to-child ratio during these projects.
